clue.text: Acrobat taking a drink.

definitions.meaning: a circus performer who does somersaults and handsprings
a flat-bottomed glass is the vessel that takes a drink

explanation.surface: A circus performer pauses for a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a gymnast who somersaults; the other is a straight-sided drinking glass.

clue.text: One advising us how to be a successful turf-layer?

definitions.text: One advising us how to be a successful turf-layer?

parts.words: One advising us how to be a successful turf-layer?
parts.note: a turf-layer reads as a gardener laying lawn, but here it is someone laying bets on the turf, the racecourse; the adviser gives racing hints

explanation.surface: A gardening expert tells us how to lay a lawn well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The turf' is horse racing, and to lay money on it is to bet; the person who sells predictions to punters is the one advising.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing adviser who sells predictions of winners to punters.

clue.text: Abroad, he keeps the Queen's peace up

definitions.text: Abroad, he keeps the Queen's peace up

parts.words: Abroad, he keeps the Queen's peace up
parts.note: an officer overseas who polices on the Queen's behalf, and does it 'up', sitting high on horseback

explanation.surface: A loyal officer serving overseas maintains order.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police serve the Crown in Canada, abroad from Britain, and are famous for patrolling on horseback, hence 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of Canada's mounted police force, a Crown officer who rides on patrol.

clue.text: Ray and Mabel's ear being bent

indicators.note: something bent is twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the S of the possessive included

explanation.surface: Ray and Mabel are going in for an ear-bending conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being bent' rearranges the letters of MABELS EAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A concentrated beam of laser light is a kind of ray.

clue.text: The newspaper experts in error?

parts.note: people who go through a newspaper, and also the proof-checking specialists whose expertise lies in spotting mistakes

explanation.surface: Have the press pundits got it wrong?
explanation.walkthrough: The public who buy a paper go through it, and proof-checkers at a publisher are experts in finding errors.
explanation.definitionFit: The audience of a newspaper, and also proof-checkers who hunt for mistakes in print.

clue.text: … it's a medicine for wind

definitions.meaning: a dose of liquid medicine to be swallowed
a current of cold air through a room

explanation.surface: Following on, this is a remedy for flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots tie the clue to the one before; 'it's a' and 'for' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a dose of liquid medicine, and a cold current of air indoors.

clue.text: Bad Seed remake made less

indicators.note: a remake of a film reworks it, so the letters are made again in a new order

explanation.surface: A remake of the film The Bad Seed was a lesser thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remake' rearranges BADSEED.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower something in value or quality is to make it less worthy.

clue.text: Gas written about in mono graph

indicators.note: about signals turning the letters round, read backwards
the letters sit inside the words mono graph

explanation.surface: A gas is described in a scientific monograph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' picks NOGRA from moNO GRAph, and 'about' turns it round; 'written' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An inert noble gas that makes up about one per cent of the air.

clue.text: A superficial coverage of Goldsmith's works

definitions.text: A superficial coverage of Goldsmith's works

parts.words: A superficial coverage of Goldsmith's works
parts.note: seems to be a shallow survey of Oliver Goldsmith's writings, but means a thin layer applied by a metalworker in gold

explanation.surface: A critic gives a shallow survey of Oliver Goldsmith's writings.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Goldsmith was an Irish author; here the goldsmith is a craftsman whose work includes laying a thin gold film over objects.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin coat of gold leaf laid over a surface, the craft of a worker in gold.

clue.text: Lunatic lets us take a pole to fights

indicators.note: a lunatic arrangement is a crazy one, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: S is short for the south pole

explanation.surface: A madman allows us to grab a pole to brawl with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunatic' rearranges LETSUS; 'take' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Scuffles and struggles are physical fights.

clue.text: Peter the First ruled here, in Germany

indicators.note: the first means only the opening letter of the name Peter is taken

parts.note: Peter the Great, Peter I, was the tsar who ruled the country of Russia

explanation.surface: A tsar's realm is placed, oddly, in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter the First' doubles as the tsar Peter I, whose realm was Russia. The definition is loose: the kingdom became the leading state within a united Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: A former kingdom in northern Germany, the dominant state of the German Empire.

clue.text: Imagined he was an air ace

definitions.text: Imagined he was an air ace

parts.words: Imagined he was an air ace
parts.note: a fictional flying hero, invented by an author rather than a man with delusions

explanation.surface: A fantasist pictured himself as a flying hero.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone daydreaming; it means a fighter pilot invented by the author W. E. Johns in his boys' adventure books.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain James Bigglesworth is the fictional fighter pilot hero of W. E. Johns's stories.

clue.text: Coach taking people up to Oxford, perhaps

definitions.text: Coach taking people up to Oxford, perhaps

parts.words: Coach taking people up to Oxford, perhaps
parts.note: looks like a bus going to Oxford, but means a private teacher preparing students to go up to a university

explanation.surface: A bus carries passengers up to Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: Going 'up' to Oxford is British idiom for starting at the university; a coach here is a private teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A private teacher who prepares students, perhaps for university entrance.

clue.text: Vital silent sea change

indicators.note: a change of these letters alters their order

explanation.surface: A calm sea turning rough matters a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges SILENTSEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Something vital is indispensable, absolutely necessary.

clue.text: Joints for jackets

definitions.meaning: short double-breasted coats of thick cloth worn by sailors

explanation.surface: Joints are made for jackets, it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for cannabis cigarettes, and short thick double-breasted coats of a naval style.

clue.text: Mothers, it's about time to get some money from the court!

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: dams are animal mothers, as in horse breeding
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Mothers decide the time has come to sue for compensation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mothers' suggests women, but dams are animal mothers in breeding. 'about' signals the container; 'it's' and 'to get' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Compensation awarded by a court to someone harmed is a sum of money.

clue.text: Knit a warm shift for writer

indicators.note: shift tells us the letters are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone knits a warm garment for an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shift' rearranges KNITAWARM; 'for' is a link word, and a shift is also a dress.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of Samuel Clemens, American author of Tom Sawyer.

clue.text: Posts pieces of paper

explanation.surface: Someone mails some sheets.
explanation.definitionFit: Upright pillars that support a building, and regular articles in a newspaper.

clue.text: He has joint control of pit loco overhaul

indicators.note: an overhaul takes something apart and rebuilds it, so these letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A man shares charge of a mine locomotive that is being serviced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overhaul' rearranges PITLOCO.
explanation.definitionFit: The second pilot on an aircraft flies it jointly with the captain.

clue.text: Having a lascivious look

parts.note: a plain description of eyeing someone with lust

explanation.walkthrough: As printed this is a plain definition with no wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle someone lustfully is to give a lewd sidelong look.

clue.text: Engineers fresh paper on board

indicators.note: being on a ship puts something inside it

parts.note: a ship one goes on board, SS for steamship

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters of paper take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Engineers put new paper down on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' is the anagram signal and 'on board' the container: being on board means inside a ship. Sappers are soldiers of Britain's Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Military engineers who dig trenches and lay or clear mines are known as sappers.

clue.text: Sailor and soldier king

parts.note: a marine is a soldier who serves at sea
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A seaman and a soldier king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaman, one who navigates or crews a ship.

clue.text: Met dire disaster-well earnt!

indicators.note: disaster wrecks the order of these letters

explanation.surface: Someone met a terrible fate that they fully deserved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' rearranges METDIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deserved has been fully earned and justified.

clue.text: Keep a sharp lookout for them in the Solent, presumably?

definitions.text: Keep a sharp lookout for them in the Solent, presumably?

parts.words: Keep a sharp lookout for them in the Solent, presumably?
parts.note: sailors near the Isle of Wight watch for a famous row of pointed chalk rocks, and the sharp lookout puns on their pointed shape

explanation.surface: Sailors in the Solent should stay alert for hazards.
explanation.walkthrough: The Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and mainland England; at the island's west tip stand three pointed chalk stacks with a lighthouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp pointed sewing tools share their name with the chalk stacks off the Isle of Wight.

clue.text: A second application for motor vehicle cover?

definitions.text: A second application for motor vehicle cover?

parts.words: A second application for motor vehicle cover?
parts.note: sounds like renewing car insurance, but means a new coat of paint applied to a car's bodywork

explanation.surface: A driver applies again for car insurance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests insurance; the application is of paint.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresh coat of paint sprayed over a car's bodywork a second time.

clue.text: Tooting man held responsible for abducting children

definitions.text: Tooting man held responsible for abducting children

parts.words: Tooting man held responsible for abducting children
parts.note: seems to be a resident of a London district accused of a crime, but means the musician of legend whose playing lured away the children of Hamelin

explanation.surface: A man from Tooting is blamed for kidnapping youngsters.
explanation.walkthrough: Tooting is a district of south London; here it means playing a pipe. The legendary piper led Hamelin's children away when the town refused to pay him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hamelin musician of legend who lured away the town's children with his music.

clue.text: It'll be a feather in your cap!

definitions.text: It'll be a feather in your cap!

parts.words: It'll be a feather in your cap!
parts.note: the idiom for an achievement taken literally, as a decorative feather worn on a hat

explanation.surface: Congratulations on a fine achievement!
explanation.walkthrough: 'A feather in your cap' is an idiom for a proud achievement; read literally it describes a decorative feather on a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A large ornamental feather, often worn as decoration on a hat or helmet.

clue.text: Those who bind in the terraces?

definitions.meaning: people who fasten things with knots or string
banked rows of seating or steps rising one above another

explanation.surface: Bookbinders work in the terraced stands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: People who fasten things with knots, and rows rising one above another like stepped seating.

clue.text: Time for our unemployment benefit

parts.note: seems to be about state welfare paid to the jobless, but means hours free from work that we can enjoy

explanation.surface: It is time to claim our dole money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unemployment benefit' looks like a state payment; here it is the benefit of not being employed, free time.
explanation.definitionFit: Free time away from work, spent as one pleases.

clue.text: Short advertising film

parts.note: a brief preview shown to promote a forthcoming movie

explanation.definitionFit: A brief preview reel promoting a forthcoming movie, shown in cinemas.

clue.text: Cat hair engulfs retreating foreign soldier

indicators.note: to engulf is to swallow up, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: GI is an American soldier, foreign from a British view

explanation.surface: A cat's coat swallows up a soldier from abroad who is in retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreating' reverses the soldier and 'engulfs' sets him inside the hair. GI is the standard crossword American soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A female tiger, the largest of the big cats.

clue.text: House rule!

definitions.meaning: a royal family line, as in the House of Windsor
a succession of rulers or period of government by one family

explanation.definitionFit: A line of hereditary rulers from one family, and the period of their reign.
